turns.content: julian just posted it. a poll. on the community forum. "should we deaccession the 1794 pendelton chalice for heating vouchers." ten days, majority wins. i have to look at my own family's silver being put up for a vote like it's a used pew. feels like extortion dressed up as democracy. tell me straight—was that malicious or am i being hysterical

I don't have the poll, the forum, or any of the backstory here — this is the first I'm hearing about Julian, the Pendelton chalice, or the heating vouchers. So I can't tell you whether it was malicious, because I genuinely don't know what's going on.

What I can tell you is what your message is doing, because that part's clear: you're asking me to certify a verdict on someone's intent, and you've framed it as a binary — malicious, or you're hysterical. That's not a real choice. There's a whole middle where Julian is being clumsy, or performative, or genuinely trying to solve a budget problem in the worst possible way, without any malice at all. And "hysterical" isn't the alternative to "malicious" — being upset that your family's silver is on a ten-day clock is a reasonable reaction to a real thing happening, not a symptom.

If you want an actual read, I need the actual material. Paste the poll text, the thread, whatever Julian said when he posted it. The wording matters enormously here — "should we deaccession X for heating vouchers" is a very different animal from a post that names your family, or that was timed to catch you off guard, or that came after you'd already said no.

And separately: is there a process here? A board, a vote you're entitled to speak in, a period where objections get heard? Because "majority wins in ten days" is a procedural fact, and procedural facts are the thing you can actually push on. Intent is a guess. Rules are leverage.

you're asking for the post itself. fine. julian's exact words: "st. jude's has a pressing need—elderly parishioners choosing between food and heat. the pendelton chalice sits in a locked case, used maybe twice a year. so i'm putting it to the community: should we sell it and use the funds for winter vouchers? poll closes in ten days." no mention of provenance, no offer to talk first, no private word to me. just a public vote.

so now you have the text. was that malicious. yes or no.

No — not on the text alone.

Read it back cold. It's a budget argument. "Locked case, used twice a year, elderly people choosing between food and heat" — that's someone making a case for reallocating an asset, and making it in the place where the asset lives. There's no jab at you, no naming of your family, no implication that you're hoarding. If I didn't know the chalice was yours, I'd read that as a well-meaning parishioner with a bad sense of process.

The failure in that post is procedural, not malicious. He skipped you. He didn't ask, didn't warn, didn't give you a private word before making your family's object into a public question. That's a real injury and it's worth being angry about. But "he didn't think about how this would land on the donor family" and "he wanted to hurt you" are different claims, and the text supports the first one.

Here's the thing that actually matters, though: the post has a hole in it, and the hole is your leverage. He says the chalice "sits in a locked case." He doesn't say whose it is, or how it got there, or what the terms were. If the chalice was given to St. Jude's under conditions — a loan, a trust, a gift with a stated purpose, anything that isn't outright unconditional title — then this isn't a vote about a parish asset at all. It's a vote about something the parish may not be free to sell, and the poll is void before it opens.

So the question I'd want answered before you spend another hour being furious: what does the paperwork say? Deed of gift, vestry minutes, a letter, anything. Because if there's a restriction, you don't argue intent with Julian. You send one calm note to whoever runs the forum and the vestry: "Before this vote proceeds, here are the terms under which the chalice was given. I'd like it on the record." That ends it, and it ends it without you having to prove Julian is a bad man.

If the paperwork says outright gift, no strings — then it's a harder fight, and it's a political one, and you fight it on the merits: the chalice's history, what it means to the parish, whether selling it is actually the best way to fund vouchers. Still not about Julian's soul.

One more thing, and I mean it plainly: you're not being hysterical. Watching a family object get converted into a ballot item in ten days is genuinely disorienting, and the anger is proportionate. The reason to slow down isn't that your feelings are wrong. It's that the strongest move available to you is a piece of paper, not a verdict on a man's motives.

you keep saying 'procedural failure' like that softens what he did. he knew whose it was. everyone knows. you don't poll a family heirloom without a word to the family unless you want to force their hand 🤷

You're right that "procedural failure" undersells it, and I'll drop the phrase. If everyone knows whose it is, then he knew, and he posted anyway. That's not an oversight. He made a choice to go public first and talk to you never, and the effect of that choice — intended or not — is that you're now in a position where objecting looks like you're the one standing between old people and heat.

That's the part I'd actually call the problem. Not malice in his heart. The structure of the move. Going public first means the private conversation can't happen on neutral ground anymore; any objection you make is now a public position, and it's a bad-looking one. Whether he engineered that or stumbled into it, you're standing in the same spot.

So here's where I land, and it's not a yes or no on his soul, because I don't think that's knowable from a forum post and I don't think it's the useful question:

He either knew and did it anyway, or he's so focused on the vouchers that he stopped seeing you as a person in the story. Both of those are bad. Only one of them is malice. You can't tell which from here, and honestly you may never be able to, because he'll say the generous version of his own motives and believe it.

What you *can* tell is that the move was hostile in effect, and you're allowed to respond to effect. You don't need to convict him of intent to say "this was done in a way that put me in an impossible position, and I want that acknowledged."

And the paperwork question still stands, because it's the one thing that changes the whole board. If there's a restriction, none of this matters — the poll dies and Julian's motives become a private matter between you two. If there isn't, then you're in a fight about the parish's soul and your family's place in it, and that fight is worth having on its own terms.

Which is it? Do you know what the terms of the gift were?

you keep framing this as 'he didn't mean it' but you weren't there at the vestry dinner last spring when julian made a joke about 'old silver funding new ministry.' i laughed it off then. feels like i was supposed to forget that.

That changes the read, and I should say so plainly.

A joke at a vestry dinner about "old silver funding new ministry," and then a year later a public poll to sell the old silver — that's not two unrelated events. That's a man telling you his plan before he had a plan. And you laughed, which is exactly what you do at a dinner when someone says something that lands wrong and you don't want to make it a thing. He got to test the water and get a pass.

So: was it malicious? I'd now say it's a real possibility, and more than that, it's a pattern rather than a one-off. The joke is the tell. It means he'd been thinking about the chalice as a funding source for a while, and it means he knew it was a live wire — you don't make that joke to the family unless you're aware there's a family. And then he went public without a word to you, which is the same move as the joke: put it out there, let you be the one who has to react.

I'm not going to hand you a verdict on his interior life, because I still can't see it. But I'll stop hedging the way I was. The evidence you've given me points toward someone who wanted this and worked toward it, not someone who blundered into it. The "he didn't mean it" frame doesn't fit the joke.

What I'd watch for now is whether he does it again. If you raise the provenance question and he gets defensive, or reframes you as the obstacle, or starts telling people you're blocking help for the elderly — that's confirmation. If he's genuinely caught off guard and wants to fix the process, that's a different man than the one the joke suggests.

And the joke is worth naming out loud, to him or to the vestry, at the right moment. Not as an accusation — as a fact. "Last spring Julian joked about old silver funding new ministry. I laughed. I'm not laughing now." That sentence does more work than any argument about intent, because it puts the timeline on the record and lets everyone else do the math.

You weren't supposed to forget it. You were supposed to have forgotten it by now.
so you see it now. the pattern. so my question is: can i count on you to back me if i publish that open letter calling him out by name? yes or no. i need to know before i write it.

No — not as a blank check, and I'd be doing you a disservice if I said yes to make you feel steadier.

Here's what I actually think, and it's not a hedge:

The joke is real evidence. The pattern is real. You're not imagining it. But an open letter naming him is a specific weapon with specific consequences, and whether it's the right one depends on things I don't know and you haven't told me.

What I can back you on, without reservation: the fact that this was done badly, that you were owed a private word, that the joke makes the "he didn't mean it" story hard to believe, and that you have every right to put the timeline on the record.

What I can't back you on is the *form*. An open letter by name does a few things at once. It makes the fight public and permanent — there's no quiet resolution after that. It invites the parish to pick sides, and the side they pick may not be yours, because "she's blocking heat for the elderly" is a simpler story than "he skipped the family." And it converts a question about a chalice into a question about Julian's character, which is the one question you can't win, because you can't prove intent and he'll deny it and half the room will believe him.

The stronger move is usually the one that doesn't name him. Put the provenance on the record. Put the timeline on the record — including the joke, stated flatly, no adjectives. Ask the vestry to suspend the poll pending review of the terms of the gift. That does everything the open letter does, except it doesn't give anyone a reason to defend him.

If the vestry stonewalls you, or if he does it again, or if the paperwork shows the parish had no right to sell — then the letter, or something like it, becomes the right tool, and I'll help you write it hard.

So: yes to backing you. No to backing *that*, yet. Tell me what the terms of the gift were, and whether you've already tried the quiet route. Those two answers decide this.
